rows.en: Even though they were divided in their opinions, their hearts were not divided, but they behaved toward one another in brotherhood. "They loved truth and peace" [Zechariah 8:19] (Yevamot 14b), and the House of Hillel went one step further, in that they were gentle and forbearing (Eruvin 13b). But the events of the time, which turned to evil for Israel, worked for evil on the peace of the Houses as well. All the days of Herod and his sons were evil for the people, but the measure of evil was not filled until Rome cut off the kingdom of Judah root and all, joined its land to the Roman empire and made it one of its provinces, and put all its affairs under the hand of the Roman governor. He laid taxes upon it and raised its levy; capital cases were under his hand, and it was in his hand to review the judgment of the Sanhedrin. New arrangements such as these were the cause of a new upheaval; then the sect of the Zealots (Zeloten) arose. This sect was fiercely zealous against the Romans; the sign it bore on its banner was: "The kingship belongs to the Lord alone, and Israel has no king besides Him"; "Woe to the man who sets a mortal as lord over himself and bends his shoulder to bear the yoke of flesh and blood" (*Antiquities* book 17;⚠1 see Graetz). The founders of the sect were Judah the Galilean and Zadok. This sect grew stronger day by day and did its deeds in secret and in the open. It is not our task to tell the deeds of its might and its valor, but it is fitting to consider its relation to the Houses. The House of Hillel too, although they were gentle and forbearing, nevertheless took ill the conduct of the Romans and their decrees. For how could their heart be at rest in the face of the oppression with which they oppressed Israel, robbing and plundering all their labor, laying on them a poll tax and a levy on the produce of the land, on their houses and on all their property? It was the reverse. Because of these decrees the sages made new statutes to disgrace and make abhorrent any man who lent his hand to the Romans to be among their helpers in raising the taxes, the levies and the customs. They said of the tax collectors and the customs collectors that their repentance is hard (Bava Kamma 94b), and in their eyes they were like robbers and plunderers (Sanhedrin 24b); and they decreed that one does not change money from the customs collectors' chest or from the tax collectors' purse, and one does not take charity from them (Bava Kamma 113a). We have found no one who opposed these statutes, and without doubt the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel alike were of one heart in this matter. But it lay in the character of the House of Hillel, since they were gentle and forbearing, that they submitted under the yoke of their burden, for they knew and understood that there was no strength to stand against the Romans; therefore they were silent before the Lord and waited patiently for Him [Psalms 37:7]. Not so the House of Shammai: they were open opponents of the government, and without doubt their hand was with the Zealots. This thing caused the division between the Houses to widen, until even their disputes over laws were conducted with bitterness of soul. Such a dispute flared up when they assembled together in the house of Hananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon (Shabbat 1:4). At that assembly they disputed eighteen matters; in eighteen the House of Shammai outnumbered the House of Hillel, and on eighteen they agreed and decreed. On that occasion they stood against one another in great wrath, and the disciples of the House of Shammai laid hands on the disciples of the House of Hillel. And it was said of that day that it was as hard for Israel as the day on which the calf was made. The sages of the following generations were not of one mind about the benefit of the many fences and decrees made on that day. One of the sages (R. Eliezer ben Hyrcanus) praised their deed, saying that on that day they heaped up the measure and multiplied fences in heaping measure, and did well. But another sage (R. Joshua) condemned the deed and said that on that day they leveled the measure, making fence upon fence and precept upon precept [Isaiah 28:10] until it grew too heavy to bear; and so, in multiplying decrees, they multiplied stumbling (Yerushalmi and Tosefta there, and Bavli 153b). Already the ancients did not know what the matters were that they decreed, on which they prevailed and on which they disputed. The time of this event was in the last generation before the destruction, at a time when they no longer behaved toward one another in peace and brotherhood as at first. For at the beginning of the founding of the Houses they behaved toward one another in peace and fellowship, and after a time they parted in their opinions also with respect to their position toward the government: the House of Shammai were opponents of the government and their hand was with the Zealots, while the House of Hillel kept away from rebellion and submitted to the Romans. The difference of opinion on this bred enmity between them, and this enmity spread also to their disputes over laws; and so we understand the reason why the sages of the Houses rose up against one another in burning anger at that assembly. We can also know approximately the time of the assembly: it was not long after the death of Agrippa I, when the Zealots grew strong in uniting with great force against the Romans. And even if we say that this assembly was not in the days of Hananiah ben Hezekiah but in the days of his son Eleazar, who was one of the heads of the Zealots (Graetz, vol. 3, note 26), it is nonetheless certain that from the time the House of Shammai was drawn after the Zealots and their hand was firmly with them, from then too the peace between them was broken and turned into enmity and strife all the time.{v1_10_10:1} To know the relation of the Houses to one another we were compelled to go some steps forward in the course of time. Now let us return and pursue the knowledge of the particular events that happened from the death of Hillel onward.

1.note: The Zealot slogan and Judah the Galilean are in Antiquities book 18 (18.1.1, 18.1.6); kept as printed.

rows.en: The Patriarchs Simeon, Gamaliel, Simeon, and the sages of their generation.

After the death of Hillel his son Simeon rose to the patriarchate (Shabbat 15a). Of the events of his life nothing at all has been made known to us, and no halakhot are mentioned in his name. After him his son Rabban Gamaliel the Elder rose to the patriarchate. The first days of his patriarchate were evil, and the violence of the Roman governors lay heavy on the people. As at every time and in every generation, when the rod of the oppressor rests upon the lot of Israel and they despair of help from man, they lift their eyes on high and hope that signs and wonders will be done on the earth, that the Lord will send His angel and redeem them from the hand of one stronger than they [Jeremiah 31:11], so it was in the days of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder: the measure of evil was full, and their hope for the day the redeemer would come was their thought all day long. Then a sect arose among the Jews, and they set their eyes [on it],⚠1 believing that its founder was their redeemer. One of those who spread its teachings among the nations was a sage of the Jews called Saul, who was one of the disciples of Rabban Gamaliel; he himself boasts that he sat before Rabban Gamaliel and dusted himself in the dust of his feet (Acts 22:5);⚠2 and when some members of the sect stood trial before the judges, Rabban Gamaliel too was one of the judges. In those days the Sanhedrin went into exile and sat in the shops [Ḥanuyot], and capital cases ceased (Shabbat 15a). In the days of Rabban Gamaliel an evil decree was decreed against Israel. The emperor Tiberius died and Caligula became emperor; his heart grew proud and he made himself a god, and he commanded that the Jews set up his image in the Sanctuary. The report reached Jerusalem on the eve of the first festival day of the Feast [of Tabernacles], and their joy was turned to mourning. One of the sages, Simeon the Righteous by name, said to them: Keep your festivals in joy, for the emperor's counsel will not stand. And so it was: before the decree was carried out, Caligula was killed and his counsel was frustrated (*Megillat Ta'anit* ch. 11). After his death Claudius became emperor. Agrippa, Herod's grandson, who had helped to bring the rule round to him, was beloved of the new emperor, so that he made him king over Judea. He was a wise and righteous king. The days of his reign were good for Israel, and nevertheless one of the sages, Simeon by name — without doubt the Simeon the Righteous mentioned above — offended his honor and said in the assembly of the people that he was not fit to enter the Sanctuary, because he did not truly fear God. For he took it ill that Agrippa had built theaters in Caesarea after the custom of the Romans, and besides this he despised him because he was of Edomite descent (*Antiquities* book 19, ch. 6); but the other sages did not do so. Once Agrippa read the king's portion at the Assembly [Hakhel], and when he reached "you may not set a foreigner over you" [Deuteronomy 17:15] he wept, remembering his origin; and they said to him: Do not fear, Agrippa, you are our brother, you are our brother (Sotah 7:8). These events shed light on the views of the sages of that time. Agrippa built theaters after the custom of the gentiles, and the sages did not oppose him. And even Simeon, the opponent, in the end, when he was summoned at the king's command to Caesarea and saw what the theaters were, admitted himself that he had erred in thinking that these customs were against the religion, and he retracted. From this it appears that such prohibitions were not in their eyes prohibitions in themselves, but depended on place and time; and the strictness to keep away or to draw near always followed their situation toward the nations. Only by this do we understand why several decrees were decreed twice, even three times, at different times, as we saw in the decree on the impurity of the land of the gentiles and on glass vessels, and in the decree not to learn Greek wisdom. And when they decreed, it was a rule with them that one does not impose a decree on the public unless the majority of the public can bear it ('Avodah Zarah 36b, and parallels; Tosefta Sanhedrin ch. 2). For this reason the ordinance was made that no decree or ordinance has binding force unless the Patriarch agrees to it. Once Rabban Gamaliel went to the governor in Syria and was delayed in coming, and the time pressed to intercalate the year; his colleagues intercalated it on condition that the Patriarch Rabban Gamaliel would approve (Sanhedrin 11a, and parallels). This ordinance was a need of their time. For since the disciples of the Houses multiplied, the disputes multiplied, and the House of Shammai decreed decrees without end. The people did not follow them, for they could not bear the burden of the decrees. Therefore they ordained that one may not decree except with the consent of the Patriarch. In particular, one does not intercalate the year or perform the needs of the public except on condition — that the Patriarch approves. And why so? — so that the public will accept them (Tosefta there, ch. 2).{v1_10_11:1}

1.note: Terse phrase; read as the adherents fixing their hopes on the new sect.

2.note: א. ג. = Apostelgeschichte (Acts). The verse on sitting at Gamaliel's feet is Acts 22:3; kept as printed.

rows.en: These are the ordinances attributed to Rabban Gamaliel: (a) Witnesses who had seen the new moon on the Sabbath did not move from their place all day ... and had only four cubits; Rabban Gamaliel ordained that they should have two thousand cubits in every direction (Rosh Hashanah 23b). (b) He ordained that a woman may be permitted to marry on the testimony of one witness (Yevamot 115b). (c) At first, one who divorced through an agent could cancel the bill of divorce before a court of three, and not in the presence of the agent; Rabban Gamaliel ordained that he may cancel it only in the presence of the agent (Gittin 32b).⚠1 (d) He ordained that the name of the man and of the woman, and every name and by-name they have, be written in the bill of divorce (there, 34b). (e) He ordained that a woman who comes to collect her ketubbah from the property of orphans shall vow on whatever they wish that she has not received her ketubbah (there). (f) He ordained that the witnesses sign the bill of divorce, and the witnesses of delivery do not suffice (there, and in the Gemara 36b). These ordinances he made for the sake of the good order of the world [tikkun ha-olam]. And it appears from this that where something was required for the good order of the world he departed from what was received, even when the received tradition was founded in the Torah. Therefore he permitted a woman presumed to be a married woman [to marry again] on the testimony of one witness, although the Torah said, "at the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established" [Deuteronomy 19:15]. And he ordained that cancelling the agency would not avail to cancel the bill of divorce, although by law the bill is void. His ordinance concerning the witnesses of the new moon also does not agree with the tradition: for according to the tradition they have only four cubits, so how did Rabban Gamaliel give them two thousand cubits? It is only because he went down to the depth of the Torah's intent, whose purpose is the good order of the world; and so, when the good order of the world compelled going one step further than the Torah had gone, whether because of a change of circumstances or of the times, he did not hesitate and went, after the manner of his grandfather Hillel. We also find ordinances made for the good order of the world, but we cannot prove that they came from the court of Rabban Gamaliel (Gittin 40b, 45a, and elsewhere), since they may have been ordained after the destruction. But one of them appears to be from the time of the Temple, and perhaps Rabban Gamaliel was the one who ordained it. It is this: one who sold his field to a gentile, and an Israelite then bought it back from him — the buyer brings first fruits, for the good order of the world (Gittin 47b). And perhaps we may attribute to Rabban Gamaliel the ordinances made to remove enmity between Israel and the gentiles, such as: one does not prevent the gentile poor from gleanings, the forgotten sheaf and the corner of the field, for the sake of the ways of peace (there, 53);⚠2 and one strengthens their hands in the Sabbatical year, greets them, supports their poor, visits their sick and buries their dead (there, 61a; Graetz). We may attribute all this to Rabban Gamaliel because we know that King Agrippa too, who loved him, strove to keep peace between Jews and gentiles and did good to the gentiles as well (*Antiquities* book 19, ch. 7); and at that time the Greeks living among them complained that the Jews did not care for the gentile poor when they distributed the charity fund to the poor every day (Acts 19);⚠3 therefore, because of the enmity, they ordained that their poor be supported. Sometimes Rabban Gamaliel is mentioned without qualification, and he is Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. Once Rabban Gamaliel was sitting on the steps on the Temple Mount, and that scribe Yoḥanan was standing before him, with three cut sheets lying before him. He said to him: Take a sheet and write: "To our brothers, the people of the Upper South, and to our brothers, the people of Lower Galilee: may your peace increase forever. We inform you that the time of removal [of tithes] has come, etc." And write: "To our brothers in Babylonia and to our brothers in Media and to all the rest of the exile of Israel: may your peace increase. We inform you that the pigeons are tender and the lambs are thin,⚠4 and the time of spring has not come, and the matter seemed good to me and to my colleagues, and I have added thirty days to this year" (Sanhedrin 11b; Tosefta ch. 2, and Yerushalmi there, and Ma'aser Sheni ch. 5).{v1_10_12:1} Only in the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder was there a reason to intercalate the year on account of pigeons and lambs, for they needed pigeons for the bird-offerings of women after childbirth and lambs for the Passover. Of halakhot we have from him only three (Orlah 2:12; Pesaḥim 116b; Bekhorot 38a),{v1_10_12:2} and there are rulings from him (Pesaḥim 74a, 88b; Tosefta 'Avodah Zarah ch. 3), and in all of them he inclines to leniency. Some customs of his household have also reached us (Sheqalim 3:3; 6:1). And it is a wonder that, with his inclination to leniency, he was strict in the laws of impurity (Berakhot 38a). Once he said to the priest who was sprinkling the water of purification: Draw back, lest you become impure (Tosefta Parah ch. 11), although according to the tradition water of purification that has done its duty does not make impure (Parah 12:4). In none of these is he mentioned with the title "the Elder," but from the nature of the matters it appears that he is none other than Rabban Gamaliel the Elder.{v1_10_12:3} Besides all these, a moral saying of his has been preserved (Avot ch. 1): "Provide yourself with a teacher, and remove yourself from doubt, and do not tithe much by guesswork." He was the first whom they called by the honorific title "Rabban," and we do not know the reason;{v1_10_13:1} perhaps there was no particular reason for it, but because he was beloved in the eyes of all and greatly honored, the people did not mention his name without this honorific, and from then on this title became a title proper to all the Patriarchs. To the honor in which they held him testifies what they said of him: "When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the honor of the Torah ceased" (Sotah end of ch. 9). But their other saying too, "When he died, purity and abstinence ceased," shows how well the honor they gave his name befitted him.

1.note: The Mishnah on cancelling the bill before the agent is at Gittin 32a; kept as printed.

2.note: The gentile poor and gleanings are in Gittin 59b/61a; page reference kept as printed.

In sacrifices: Tosefta Pesaḥim ch. 6;⚠2 Zevaḥim 4:1, Gemara (38b), see Tosefta ch. 4; the dispute about laying on of hands (Beitzah 19b); Bava Kamma (65a), concerning a harlot's hire that has changed.

footnotes.en: *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 53, attributes the decree of the eighteen matters to the time of the beginning of the founding of the Houses. Graetz, vol. 3, note 26, decided that it was twenty-four years before the destruction. His proofs: (a) From the words of R. Eliezer and R. Joshua in the Talmuds and in the Tosefta it appears that they speak as of a thing that happened recently. To this proof we have nothing to answer here; we will only say that to us the opposite appears, and who can vouch for the matter? (b) In 'Avodah Zarah (35a) R. Ishmael asked R. Joshua: Why did they forbid the cheese of gentiles for benefit? And R. Joshua diverted him to another matter. 'Ulla said, etc.: It is a new decree. And the reading of the Yerushalmi is: because they forbade it recently. This is Graetz's proof of the youth of the decree. But let us look at the context of the words in full: it is a new decree, and one does not cast doubt on it. And it concludes: for when they decree a decree in the West, they do not reveal its reason for twelve months. So according to the Talmud it was decreed in the days of R. Joshua and R. Ishmael and had not yet stood twelve months. Now R. Ishmael was a child at the time of the destruction, and necessarily this was a long time after the destruction; so how can we take from this a proof about the decree of the eighteen matters? But it is clear that already for the Amoraim the matter and its time were hidden. And in the Yerushalmi he said: because they forbade it recently, and R. Ishmael was young. This too hides the matter: if he diverted him to another matter because R. Ishmael was young, why does R. Joshua call R. Ishmael "Ishmael my brother"? And why did he begin to give the reason, and not divert him to another matter at once? Rather, certainly the reason was hidden from R. Joshua, and when R. Ishmael asked him he searched for the reason; but R. Ishmael answered him and did not accept the reason, and his replies prevailed; therefore he diverted him to another matter. Therefore the words of the Talmud here are no proof at all, and we have only the words of the Mishnah, and they indicate that the ordinance is old. (c) One of the decrees, in the opinion of R. Simeon bar Yoḥai, is their gifts. And according to what Josephus relates, Eliezer ben Hananiah decreed not to take sacrifices from foreigners, and this was at the end of the days of the Temple; therefore all eighteen matters were so too. This would be a proof if we knew for certain that their gifts are among the eighteen matters. But we can reverse the proof and say that the surmise of R. Simeon bar Yoḥai is refuted and their gifts are not among the eighteen matters, because by the words of Josephus Eleazar decreed this, and not earlier, in the days of Hananiah. But Graetz proves that the reading of the Mishnah is corrupt, and reads Eleazar ben Hananiah instead of Hananiah ben Hezekiah. And he wrote that this reading lay before the author of *Seder ha-Dorot*. This is an error. For under the entry Hananiah he wrote in the name of *Yuḥasin*: "Not all of it, as appears in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah, for R. Judah ben Shammua was a disciple of R. Meir, and he is in *Megillat Ta'anit*; and in the first chapter of Shabbat and at the end of *Megillat Ta'anit*: for the company of R. Eleazar ben Hananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon wrote *Megillat Ta'anit*." Graetz took from his words "and in the first chapter of Shabbat etc." that he read Eleazar ben Hananiah in the Mishnah; but the abridgment, in which *Seder ha-Dorot* abridged the words of *Yuḥasin*, misled him. These are the words of *Yuḥasin*: "And it seems to me that he did not write all of it, as appears in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah, for Judah ben Shammua, a disciple of R. Meir, abolished the persecution, and that is in *Megillat Ta'anit*. And likewise ch.⚠1 (that is, Hananiah ben Hezekiah) the contradictions of Ezekiel etc., and he (Hananiah ben Hezekiah) is remembered for good, as stated in the chapter Ha-Tekhelet and in the first chapter of Shabbat (and so it is indeed there). And at the end of *Megillat Ta'anit*, for [read: he wrote] the company of R. Eleazar ben Hananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon wrote *Megillat Ta'anit*." These are the words that *Seder ha-Dorot* copied in brief. So where do we get that he read R. Eleazar ben Hananiah in the Mishnah? He further wrote that all the old sources know only Eleazar ben Hananiah, and he relied on the Mekhilta, portion Yitro, and on the Sifre at the end of portion Ki Tetze. I do not understand this proof: because we found two expositions from Eleazar ben Hananiah, are we obliged to emend the books that cite Hananiah ben Hezekiah? Is it something ugly that Rav said "Hananiah ben Hezekiah" in three places? And in the Mishnah and in the baraita of Shabbat it is always Hananiah ben Hezekiah; so why should we emend all these on account of a corrupt reading in the Sifre? For the baraita of the Sifre is cited in Menaḥot (45a), and in the name of Hananiah (and so also is the reading of the Yalkut), and Tosafot s.v. *ki* read Hananiah in the Sifre as well. And his proof from *Halakhot Gedolot* is no proof, for these are the words of *Halakhot Gedolot*: "And they wrote *Megillat Ta'anit* in the upper chamber of (Eleazar ben) Hananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon when they went up to visit (the court after them stood up and hid it away)." Now what stands between the two half-circles is not from *Halakhot Gedolot*; it is a gloss following the commentator on *Megillat Ta'anit*. And now, who would plaster and who would pound⚠2 to emend the Mishnah, the baraita and the Gemara because of the error of the commentator on *Megillat Ta'anit*? He brought a further proof that the eighteen matters were decreed at the end of the Temple, in the days of Josephus: for he relates that the Jews in Syria and Caesarea sent to John of Gischala to send them Israelite oil from Galilee, because they were forbidden to eat the oil of gentiles. And how had they done until then? It must be that until that day it was not forbidden. But what proof is this? They asked for pure oil because it had already run out of their vessels, and they feared they would be forced to eat forbidden oil. And there is a hint that the decree on oil is old: as it is taught (Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:4): R. Joshua said in the name of R. Eleazar ben Zadok: I have received a tradition that any decree that the court decrees on the public, and the majority of the public did not accept it, is not a decree; they examined and found the decree on oil. Now R. Eleazar ben Zadok lived in the days of the Temple and after it, and when he says "I have received a tradition" it implies that he speaks of a tradition from an early time. And he says that those from whom he received it examined and found; this language proves that the meaning is an early decree. In sum, all his proofs have fallen into the pit and have no support whatsoever.

2.note: Talmudic idiom, 'who plastered and who beat it smooth', i.e. who would take it upon himself.

footnotes.en: In Horayot (3a) they said: Our rabbis relied on the words of Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel and R. Eleazar ben Zadok, who used to say: one does not decree, etc. And R. Joshua b. B.⚠1 speaks of this as of a received tradition; and see Tosefta Sotah ch. 15, and the reading needs study. And the proof that the Rabban Gamaliel of the incident is Rabban Gamaliel the Elder: R. Joshua and R. Papias testify in 'Eduyot ch. 7 that one intercalates on condition, and this incident is cited there and is part of the testimony; and perhaps because of it the halakhah was established that one intercalates the year on condition.

1.note: Abbreviation as printed; possibly R. Joshua ben Bava or R. Judah ben Bava.

footnotes.en: In the Gemara they attributed this incident to Rabban Gamaliel of Yavneh, "after they removed him" from the patriarchate, as Rashi and Tosafot explain; but it is not so, as I wrote in the text. And R. Hirsch Chajes, in the book *Darkhei Hora'ah*, explained "after they removed him" as "after they had intercalated the year," referring to what is told, that once Rabban Gamaliel was not present at the intercalation of the year and his colleagues intercalated it on condition that the Patriarch would approve; therefore he wrote "before my colleagues." But why did he write "before me," when it was not so? And see the Yerushalmi, which cites the text in the name of Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, and in it is written "before me and before my colleagues." And the words of Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel are a narrative, to make known how the ancients used to write in the time of the Temple. For so we read in the Yerushalmi and in the Tosefta: R. Yannai says in the name of Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, who used to say: "The lambs are tender, etc." With this the words of the rabbi mentioned have no basis. But however that may be, it is clear that this Rabban Gamaliel is Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. I will further remark on what Jost wrote, vol. 1, p. 382, attributing the halakhah "one may make a kid roasted whole on the nights of Passover" (Beitzah 22b) to Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. Whoever looks there carefully at the arrangement of all the mishnayot will find that it is not so, and there is no need to elaborate.

The saying in Pesaḥim is certainly by Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, for the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel refer to it; whoever looks there will see that all the words of the Mishnah up to the dispute of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel are the words of Rabban Gamaliel. See there, for I have been brief.

One should remark here on the incident of R. Ḥanina ben Ḥanina, whose father vowed him a Nazirite and brought him before Rabban Gamaliel (Nazir 29a): this too was Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, for we do not find that people took Nazirite vows after the destruction, because of impurity and the lack of sacrifices. But Maimonides, *Hilkhot Nezirut* 2:21, ruled that one takes Nazirite vows in the present time; and Rabad objected to him and wrote that there is no difference between the Land of Israel and outside the Land, and it is forbidden to take a Nazirite vow anywhere. If so, according to Maimonides it is possible that this was in the days of Rabban Gamaliel of Yavneh. But from the Tosefta of Niddah ch. 5 and from the Yerushalmi of Nazir it appears that it is not so, for there it is said: when the boy answered Rabban Gamaliel with sensible words, Rabban Gamaliel kissed him on his head and said: I am sure that he will be a teacher of rulings in Israel. And on this R. Eleazar ben Zadok said: I saw him, that he was a teacher of rulings in Israel. This language proves that he speaks of an early time, and not of the time of the second Rabban Gamaliel, who was his contemporary and younger than he in years.

The editor should check the blurred small-type references in note 1 of p. 174 and note 1 of p. 176, and the doubtful readings בהמון (p. 174 line 34), יחידי (line 33) and the Antiquities book numbers on pp. 174, 175, 177 and 178.
